message.content: In lions, one of the most striking examples of a dominant genetic trait is the presence of a mane in adult males. The genes that control mane development are expressed dominantly, meaning that a single copy of the relevant allele (often linked to high levels of testosterone) is enough to produce the full mane phenotype. In contrast, females and cubs typically lack a mane because they do not carry the dominant allele or because it is not expressed until puberty. This dominant expression of mane growth is a classic example of how a single allele can dictate a major physical characteristic in a species.
